idiom_name: access-level modifiers (private/fileprivate/internal) + guard type whose stored resource is private
implementation_notes: Swift's realization is its access-control system: private 'restricts the use of an entity to the enclosing declaration, and to extensions of that declaration that are in the same file', fileprivate restricts it to the file, internal is the module default, and the governing rule is that 'no entity can be defined in terms of another entity that has a lower (more restrictive) access level' - so a public guard type can hold a private resource but cannot publish it through a public property or function signature. The classic proxy collapses into a struct/class with private stored state and public methods that check the policy before touching the resource; a public type defaults to internal members, so the guard's surface is widened deliberately, and a factory (not the caller) has to construct it because the resource type may not appear in public API. The compiler enforces all of this at compile time; the documented widening is testing (@testable import reaches internal entities), and there is no runtime gate, so the process/OS boundary carries the security claim against code you did not compile.
pitfalls: Access levels are compile-time only: the Swift runtime does not stop unsafe pointer tricks or code compiled into the same module, and @testable widens internal entities for tests - private is not a sandbox.

The lower-access rule forbids publishing the resource type in a public signature, so the guard must be built by a factory that takes the policy and obtains the resource internally - plan the construction path, not just the accessors.
Extensions in the same file share private access, so a helper extension can bypass the checks; keep extensions that touch the resource inside the guard's file and deliberately minimal.
Returning the resource through a public computed property or a leaking accessor re-opens the path; return copies or views, and remember that a leaked class reference is not re-checkable.
